opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, that's a question we spent a lot of time on, and the honest answer is that you often don't want to decide upfront. Different models have different strengths. Some frontier models are great at bold, structural rewrites. Smaller, cheaper models are often perfectly fine at local tweaks like changing a hyperparameter or fixing an edge case. And you usually don't know in advance which one will be most useful for a given problem, or even at a given stage of the search.

So what we've found works well is treating model selection as a bandit problem. You keep an ensemble of LLMs, and each time you need a mutation you sample one according to a policy that tracks how much each model has actually contributed. Did its proposals improve fitness relative to the parent? Did they compile and pass the evaluator at all? Over time the search shifts its budget toward the models that are paying off, but you keep some exploration, because the best model early on isn't necessarily the best later. Early on you might want big conceptual jumps, and later you're refining, and a different model might shine there.

Cost matters a lot too. If one model is ten times more expensive and only marginally better at producing improvements, you'd rather call the cheap one more often and sample more candidates. Evolutionary search rewards diversity and volume, so it's really improvement per dollar, or per evaluation, that you care about, not raw per-call quality.

And there's a diversity argument. Models from different families have different priors and different failure modes. Mixing them gives you a more varied set of mutations, which helps keep the population from collapsing onto one idea. So my short answer: don't pick one, pick a portfolio, and let the search tell you how to weight it.

r002.rationale: It attributes improvements to the model whose proposals improved fitness; it does not describe ambiguity caused by an earlier mutation serving as a stepping stone.

r003.rationale: It explicitly frames model selection as a bandit problem, with an ensemble of models sampled by a policy that tracks each model’s contributions.

r004.rationale: It tracks improvement relative to a parent, but does not adapt selection probabilities based on performance on similar parent nodes.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a question I think about a lot, because honestly the choice of model turns out to be one of the most consequential hyperparameters in the whole pipeline, and it's also one of the least principled parts of how people do this right now.

So let me give you the practical answer first, and then the slightly more philosophical one. The practical answer is that you almost never want a single model. In the systems we've built, like the AI Scientist lineage and the more recent evolutionary coding work, we run an ensemble, and we sample from it with some probability distribution. Part of that is just robustness. Every model has its own quirks, its own biases about what kind of code it likes to write, its own failure modes. If you only use one model, your search inherits all of that structure, and you end up exploring a very narrow region of program space. Mixing models gives you more diverse mutations, and diversity is really the lifeblood of evolutionary search. The whole thing dies if your population collapses onto one basin.

The second practical consideration is cost versus capability, and this is where it gets interesting. You're going to be making thousands, maybe tens of thousands, of calls. So you can't just throw the most expensive frontier model at every single mutation. What we've found works well is a kind of tiered approach. You use cheaper, faster models for the bulk of the proposals, the exploitation phase where you're making small local edits, tweaking a hyperparameter, refactoring a loop. And then you reserve the stronger models for the moments where you need a genuine conceptual leap, where the population has plateaued and you need something that actually reads the whole history and says, okay, everything we've tried in this direction is saturating, let's try a fundamentally different algorithm.

And actually, you can make that adaptive. You can treat the model selection itself as something like a bandit problem. You track which model's proposals are getting accepted into the archive, which ones are producing fitness improvements, and you shift your sampling toward whatever is working on this particular task. Because it really is task-dependent. For some problems the smaller models are totally sufficient and the big model is just burning money. For others, the small models just keep proposing the same three ideas over and over.

Now the more philosophical point. I think there's a tendency to anthropomorphize this and say, well, the smarter model will obviously propose better mutations. But that's not quite right in an evolutionary framing. The model isn't the optimizer. The selection pressure is the optimizer. The model is more like the mutation operator, and what you want from a mutation operator is a good balance of locality and surprise. Sometimes a model that is, let's say, less careful, that makes slightly weirder edits, actually gives you better exploration. There's a real sense in which being a bit sloppy is a feature. So the question isn't just which model is smartest, it's which distribution over edits gives you the best search dynamics for your fitness landscape. And that's an empirical question that I don't think anyone has a clean theory for yet, which is frankly what makes it fun.

r001.rationale: The response discusses choosing models by task and capability but does not mention SWE-bench or say that its top-performing model may be unsuitable for mutation proposals.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss uncertainty about whether a later gain came from its proposing model or from an earlier mutation that enabled it.

r003.rationale: It calls adaptive selection “something like a bandit problem,” but does not frame it as a multi-armed bandit with each model as an arm.

r004.rationale: It proposes favoring models whose mutations improve fitness, but does not condition that adaptation on improvements from similar parent nodes.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is to evaluate the model inside the search loop. You’re not necessarily looking for the model that writes the best program in one shot. You’re looking for a model that, given a parent program and some feedback, proposes useful variations reliably.

There are a few trade-offs there. How often does it produce valid code? How often does a mutation improve the objective? And how diverse are those mutations? A model that keeps proposing the same reasonable solution can actually be quite limiting for evolutionary search.

Then you have to factor in cost and latency. A stronger model might give you better individual proposals, but a smaller, faster model might let you explore many more candidates. Which one wins also depends on how expensive it is to evaluate each program. If evaluations are expensive, it makes sense to spend more on generating a good candidate.

So I would compare models under a fixed budget on representative tasks and look at the progress of the search, rather than just a coding benchmark. Ultimately, the thing you care about is the combination of the model, the mutation prompt, and the evolutionary algorithm.

r001.rationale: The response recommends evaluating models in the search loop rather than by coding benchmarks, but it does not mention frontier models or SWE-bench or make the stated comparison.

r002.rationale: It discusses measuring whether mutations improve the objective, but not the ambiguity of crediting a later gain to its proposer versus an earlier model that supplied a stepping stone.

r003.rationale: It does not frame model selection as a multi-armed bandit or represent models as arms.

r004.rationale: It does not describe adapting selection probabilities based on prior gains from similar parent nodes.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you have to evaluate the model in the context of the search loop. It’s not necessarily the model that scores highest on a coding benchmark. What you care about is whether it proposes mutations that are valid, diverse, and actually improve the programs you’re evolving.

So I would take a representative set of programs, give different models the same mutation budget, and measure what happens after executing and evaluating their proposals. How often do they produce runnable code? How often do they improve fitness? And what does that cost in tokens and wall-clock time?

There’s a trade-off there: a stronger model might make better proposals, but a smaller, faster model might let you explore many more candidates. The useful comparison is the progress your search makes under a fixed budget. And that can change over the course of a run—making small local edits and proposing a substantial algorithmic change may benefit from different models.
